chunks: "Magnetic current sensing measures the field a current makes instead of the voltage it drops, so there's no resistor in the path. There are three main versions.
A Hall-effect sensor puts a thin semiconductor plate near the conductor.
The field deflects carriers and produces a small voltage proportional to the field, which is proportional to the current. It works at DC and AC, and it's isolated.
A current transformer uses the conductor as a one-turn primary and a secondary of N turns, so the secondary current is I p over N , and a burden resistor turns that into a voltage.
It's rugged and nearly lossless, but AC only. A Rogowski coil is an air-core coil that outputs M dI over dt , so you integrate it.
It can't saturate, so it's great for huge fast currents, but also AC only. The pros are isolation, almost no insertion loss, and high current range.
The cons are cost, size, offset and gain drift, stray-field sensitivity, and limited accuracy at small currents.
So I'd use them for isolation or high current, and use a shunt when I can."
